title: You've joined a team with little documentation and no tests. How do you get productive — and earn trust?
description: A structured onboarding plan for a codebase nobody documented: read the seams, ship small, leave every place better, and turn your fresh-eyes advantage into value.

data.text: **Question:** You've joined a team with little documentation and no tests. How do you get productive — and earn trust?

Treat the onboarding as a deliberate project: run the app end-to-end first, use your fresh eyes to document what veterans can no longer see, take the smallest real task that touches many layers, and add characterization tests around the code you modify. Trust comes from shipping small, verified changes quickly — not from big refactors in week one. Your unique asset is being the only person who still remembers what confused you; write that down as you go.

**Week 1–2 — Map before you touch:**
- Get the whole stack running locally; if setup is painful, that first pull-request fixing the README/dev script is a real contribution
- Trace one request end-to-end (endpoint → service → DB) and write it up — you're the only one who can still see the forest
- Learn the deploy path and where the dashboards live: you can't be productive in code you can't ship or observe
- Ask 'why is it like this?' constantly — the answers are the undocumented architecture (often historical, sometimes wise)

**Week 2–4 — Ship the small slice:** pick a task that is low-risk but crosses several layers (a field through API, validation, DB, UI). It forces you to learn the real conventions — naming, error handling, where logic belongs — far better than reading.

**The trust playbook:**
- Small PRs, clearly described, tests included — reviewers relax quickly
- Add *characterization tests* around the code you change: they pin current behavior (even quirky behavior) so your change provably doesn't regress it
- Fix one papercut per task (a confusing name, a missing log line) — the Boy Scout rule, at low risk
- Publicly credit the teammates who unblocked you

**What to avoid:** the week-three rewrite proposal (you don't yet know why the weird code exists), silent heroics, and judging the codebase aloud — it's their scar tissue.

data.title: Turn onboarding into content
data.text: Every question you had to ask a teammate is a question the next hire will have. Convert your notes into the first real documentation the repo has had — and you've demonstrated ownership before your probation review.

Interviewers assess:
- Structure: map → small slice → expand, not random flailing
- Pragmatism about tests: characterization tests to make change safe, not demanding a greenfield rewrite
- Interpersonal awareness: asking why, crediting people, avoiding 'your code is a mess'
- Self-sufficiency balanced with knowing when to ask

items: Proposing big rewrites before understanding historical constraints
Waiting to be fully productive before contributing anything
Not writing down what confused you — losing the fresh-eyes advantage forever
Shipping large unreviewed changes because 'there are no tests to stop me'
Treating the lack of documentation as someone else's failure instead of your first opportunity
How do characterization tests differ from conventional unit tests?
What if the team pushes back on adding tests to everything you touch?
How do you prioritize which part of an unfamiliar codebase to learn first?
How would you pitch writing documentation to a team that 'never has time'?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Run the stack, trace one request, learn the deploy path first
Ship a small cross-layer task; add characterization tests around it
Write down your fresh-eyes questions as the team's first documentation
Avoid week-three rewrites and codebase bashing
data.takeaway: In an undocumented codebase, the newest engineer is the only one who can still see the gaps — turning those gaps into docs and tests is how trust is earned.
